newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope voices love for Poland at end of visit home.
newsitem.headline: Pope voices love for Poland at end of visit home.

text.p: Saying his love for Poland was still burning despite nearly 20 years in the Vatican, Pope John Paul celebrated mass for more than half a million people on Tuesday at the end of a triumphant visit to his homeland.
"Years spent in Rome have not extinguished my love for this land," the Pope, his face full of emotion, told the crowd filling the airport runways in the southeastern town of Krosno.
"May God reward you. Now it is time to go back to work in Rome," he said as the crowd chanted "Stay with us," in a rapturous send-off at the last major event of the 11-day visit.
At the mass the Pope canonised 15th century Franciscan holy man John of Dukla, who helped his people repel a Tartar attack on Lvov, now part of Ukraine, in 1474.
In his sermon the Pope praised the saint for his patriotism, as well as modern church leaders who had stood up to communism in this century.
He urged Poles, particularly those in rural areas, to hold on to their 1,000-year-old Christian traditions in the face of mounting secularism including that spread by the mass media.
"Do not let them be taken away from you. Some people are trying to do so. The world is full of dangers," the Pope said.

The crowd was the second largest of the trip, after a mass which drew more than 1.5 million to Krakow on Sunday, and the church estimates a total of six million people flocked to see the Pope during his journey through the west and south.

In Poland, the 77-year-old Pope has repeatedly paid tribute to the faithful and the church hierarchy for holding fast while Marxist regimes before 1989 curtailed church freedom and denied permission to build new places of worship.
He challenged Poles to ponder how they should use freedoms he helped them to win through his support for the Solidarity free trade union's struggle for democracy against communism.
The Pope was flying by helicopter to Krakow on Tuesday afternoon and returning to Rome in the evening.
"He is not a sentimental man...but he has a strong capacity to be moved by emotions," chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said when asked if the Pope was sad at the thought of leaving.

The last leg of the trip through 12 towns and cities took the Pope to the highlands near his birthplace of Wadowice, and to Krakow where he rose from student to cardinal and which he left in 1978 for his unexpected election as Pontiff.

On Monday he prayed at the grave in Krakow of his mother, father and brother whose loss before he was 21 hurt him deeply. Earlier, visiting his former university, he recalled the day wartime Nazi occupiers took its professors to a concentration camp.
John Paul repeatedly told his compatriots their freedom was meaningless if not shaped by moral values.
On June 3 in Gniezno, where the presidents of seven nations gathered to hear him, the Pope also warned of an invisible new wall of "economic and political selfishness" dividing Europe.
Nowhere did the Pope challenge current Polish values more strongly than over the law, introduced last year, allowing abortion in cases of a woman's financial or other hardship.
He said societies allowing abortion were barbarous and on Monday he praised doctors who refused to conduct abortions which the Catholic Church views as the killing of children.
In Krosno, among gifts presented to the Pope after the mass, were signed pledges from doctors at local hospitals not to carry out abortions.

The Pope's words on this and other issues addressed highly politicised matters amid early campaigning for parliamentary elections around September that pit pro-Catholic, anti-abortion rightist opposition parties against the ruling ex-communists.

Although rightist groups gathered around Solidarity hope the impact of the Pope's visit will help bring them victory, even chiefs of the ex-communists paid tribute to the calming effects of his presence on political rows raging in Poland.
